Recipes and examples

This page is about choosing a project shape and getting it shipped. For source followed by live output, open the live showcase. For the component and SDK lookup tables, use the API cheatsheet.

Start with a static site 

slamhaus init my-site
cd my-site
slamhaus check --strict
slamhaus build
slamhaus serve

Use this for a portfolio, studio page, release notes, documentation, blog, or small project site. It produces HTML and CSS with no browser runtime.

Generate the built-in examples

The minimal profile demonstrates portable Markdown and a clean project layout:

slamhaus examples static-site --profile minimal

The complete profile includes typed UI, C++, WebAssembly, canvas metadata, mobile behavior, and PWA configuration:

slamhaus examples wasm-site --profile complete
cd wasm-site
slamhaus toolchain install
slamhaus build

Choose the smallest useful page 

release notes / docs / blog       -> .md
metadata or Slam UI               -> .slam
small event function              -> cpp wasm fence
growing behavior                  -> code/<module>.cpp
site-wide navigation/footer       -> partials/
interactive toy or tool           -> .slam + typed C++

A practical project layout 

my-site/
├── slamhaus.yaml
├── AGENTS.md
├── pages/
│   ├── index.slam
│   └── notes.md
├── partials/
│   ├── navigation.md
│   └── footer.md
├── assets/
│   └── site.css
├── code/
│   └── tools.cpp
└── dist/

slamhaus.yaml records the compiler version, site metadata, theme styles, and layout partials. AGENTS.md keeps the project's local working agreements close to the source.

Build a docs site

Keep the content ordinary Markdown and add front matter only where it helps:

---
title: Rendering notes
description: Experiments and decisions from the graphics lab.
tags: [graphics, tools]
toc: true
---
# Rendering notes

The page remains portable GFM and can be reviewed without a compiler.

Add a custom stylesheet under assets/, then reference it from the project:

theme:
  styles: [assets/site.css]

Build a browser tool

Use the live showcase as the starting point for forms, calculators, and small tools. The usual flow is:

  1. Declare named controls and outputs in Slam UI.
  2. Bind an event to a namespace-scope C++ function.
  3. Run slamhaus check --strict.
  4. Build with the pinned Emscripten toolchain.
  5. Test the generated HTML and WASM module in a browser.

The compiler generates the bridge and validates argument conversion. You do not maintain selectors, event glue, or a separate frontend build.

Build a small game-like interaction

The live maze demonstrates the useful split: C++ owns state and movement rules, while Slam UI owns the board output and keyboard/mobile controls. The same pattern works for a quiz, level editor, inventory panel, debug console, or interactive fiction tool.

Deploy to GitHub Pages

The repository's preferred deployment publishes committed dist/ output:

./scripts/build-pages.sh
git add dist
git commit -m "Regenerate site"

The script uses the local Emscripten cache and rewrites local runtime/module URLs for project Pages paths. GitHub Actions can rebuild manually, but committed output is the recommended release path.

Development loop 

slamhaus check . --strict
slamhaus fmt . --check
cmake --build build --parallel
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

Use slamhaus language-schema and slamhaus lsp when integrating with an editor. Use slamhaus doctor when the compiler or Emscripten toolchain needs diagnosis.

Why these examples are deliberately small

Slamhaus is designed for composition: readable pages, a few typed behaviors, and a deployable result. When a project grows, move shared behavior into normal C++ modules and keep each page's Slam UI close to the content it controls.
